disclosure: Show only after an incorrect response. Never use as a pre-answer prompt or substitute for the user's explicit hint. Preserve initial response and attempt number.

u1-01.text: Look again at the marked stone and check whether each counted point is both empty and directly adjacent.

u1-02.text: Recount the intersections next to this edge stone. A neighbouring position must actually be on the board.

u1-03.text: Compare the corner with the centre: how many neighbouring intersections can a stone reach from here?

u1-04.text: Treat the two connected stones as one group. Check your list for repeated empty intersections.

u1-05.text: Try tracing a path between the marked stones using direct contacts along the lines. Is that path there already?

u1-06.text: Your move did not capture the marked white stone. Check the group's liberties after that move rather than following a diagonal.

u1-07.text: The white stone is still on the board. Recheck which empty intersections actually touch it at the edge.

u1-08.text: The target still has room. Check the empty neighbours within the corner, without counting points beyond the board.

u1-09.text: The two white stones are one group. Recount the empty intersections touching either stone, counting shared points only once.

u1-10.text: Black remains in danger after that move. Compare the connected group's liberties before and after your extension.

u2-01.text: Look for a chain of same-colour stones joining the marked pair through direct horizontal or vertical contacts.

u2-02.text: Trace the group between the marked stones, including direct contacts above and below.

u2-03.text: Consider whether the stones actually touch along a line now, rather than whether they could support one another later.

u2-04.text: Follow the board line between the black stones and check whether every intermediate stone is also black.

u2-05.text: After your move, are the two marked black stones joined by a continuous chain of touching black stones?

u2-06.text: Check the connection after playing: can you trace directly from the upper stone to the lower one?

u2-07.text: Recheck whether your new stone directly touches both of the marked black stones despite their closeness to the edge.

u2-08.text: Your move has not occupied the direct connection route in this task. Trace the shortest line between White's two marked stones.

u2-09.text: Consider the line from the upper white stone to the lower one. Which connection route is your move actually blocking?

u2-10.text: The proposed move did not block White's specified direct connection. Check the board line joining the marked stones.

u4-m01.text: After that move, look at the empty space still inside Black's surrounding stones. Have you created two separate enclosed points, or is the space still joined?

u4-m02.text: The orientation has changed, but the local reading task has not. Recheck whether your move separates the remaining eye space into two parts.

u4-m03.text: Imagine White replying in this straight-three space. Does your move take away White's chance to create two distinct eyes, or leave that chance open?

u4-m04.text: Check the shape after rotating it. Your move should interfere with the two-eye plan, not merely occupy another nearby intersection.

u4-m05.text: One of Black's eyes is already secure. Look at the other candidate eye and check which of its surrounding points still need Black's support.

u4-m06.text: Read the vertical shape as an eye-boundary task. After your move, is the unfinished eye enclosed on every necessary side?

u4-m07.text: White already has one completed eye. Examine the incomplete eye space and whether your move prevents its enclosing boundary from being finished.

u4-m08.text: Do not treat the rotated board as a different rule. Recheck which part of White's second eye is still unfinished after your move.

u3-01.text: Judge the position after the move, including any captures. Would Black's group have a neighbouring empty point if no opposing stones were removed?

u3-02.text: Look at the full move sequence, not only the occupied point. Recheck what happens to neighbouring White stones before counting Black's liberties.

u3-03.text: Imagine both players immediately taking the same stone back in turn. What problem would that cause for the game?

u3-04.text: Distinguish an immediate recapture from a move elsewhere. Which action would recreate the preceding board position on this very turn?

u3-05.text: A threat played away from the ko matters only if the opponent has a real reason to answer it. Reconsider the role of that move in the exchange.

u3-06.text: Check the rule taught and enforced in this specific interactive engine. Do not assume every possible repetition rule is supported.

u4-01.text: Focus on whether White can safely occupy both enclosed points, not on the total number of stones surrounding the group.

u4-02.text: Consider what an opponent might do when there is only one enclosed eye space. Would the status be settled without reading any replies?

u4-03.text: Consider how the same eye-shaping intersection matters to each player. The question is about a shared local target, not move order alone.

u4-04.text: Test the eye-shaped space by imagining a legal opponent move there. Would entering that point be possible without immediately losing the stone?

u4-05.text: Look for a change to eyes, liberties or a connection, then ask what the other player would do. Avoid relying on appearance alone.

u4-06.text: Pay attention to the player-to-move condition. Would the same local sequence still be available if the opponent played first?

u5-01.text: Compare how quickly the two board sizes let you reach different stages of a game. The underlying rules do not change with the smaller board.

u5-02.text: Think about room for your stones to develop after the first few moves. Is an immediate local chase necessarily the best opening goal?

u5-03.text: The endangered group and the small corner offer different kinds of value. Check the cost if you ignore the more urgent position.

u5-04.text: Look at what remains undecided: major group survival or the last territorial boundaries? The phase depends on the work still needed.

u5-05.text: Recall the usual end-of-game procedure after both players decide there is no useful move. Do not confuse finishing with restarting.

u5-06.text: Choose a question tied to a decision you could recognise again. A useful review should identify something observable on a future board.

u6-01.text: Picture how many sides of an area need surrounding near a corner compared with the middle. Do not mistake efficiency for a guaranteed best move.

u6-02.text: Consider the support your existing corner stone provides and what your new stone could help it accomplish. Distance alone is not the target.

u6-03.text: Compare the purpose of each opening point in relation to nearby stones. A universal claim needs more than one familiar pattern.

u6-04.text: Before extending, look at the friendly and opposing stones already nearby. Ask what room and pressure each direction creates.

u6-05.text: The large space may remain available while the threatened group may not. Compare the consequences of delaying each option.

u6-06.text: After a development move, ask what it contributes to the surrounding position. Do not judge it only by immediate captures.

u7-01.text: Try drawing the boundary of the proposed area. Would both players agree it is relatively settled, or could either still contest it?

u7-02.text: Think about a group's stability and its ability to support nearby play. Thickness is not the same as a tally of secured points.

u7-03.text: Consider where a strong wall can influence later play. Its value cannot be read from the number of stones alone.

u7-04.text: The immediate territory is only one side of the exchange. Reconsider what the opponent could gain from the outward-facing strength.

u7-05.text: Check which side has nearby support before starting a fight beside the wall. Do not assume a wall changes the rules of liberties.

u7-06.text: Ask which whole-board factors make thickness useful in this position. A fixed formula is unlikely to describe every wall.

u8-01.text: Compare eye space, escape routes and nearby support for each group. A group's current liberty count alone may not tell the whole story.

u8-02.text: An attack may create useful pressure even if the stones escape. Revisit what your own position might gain during the chase.

u8-03.text: One group faces an immediate danger while the opponent has a separate weakness. Check whose threatened loss can happen on the next turn.

u8-04.text: Follow the likely escape route and notice which of your groups can support the chase. The direction matters more than appearances.

u8-05.text: The opponent may now be safe. Check whether another attacking move gains anything or instead exposes your own stones.

u8-06.text: Imagine the opponent finding a stronger defence than the one you hope for. Is there still a benefit to starting the attack?

u9-01.text: Your candidate move is only the first part of a sequence. Try reading the reply that most seriously challenges it.

u9-02.text: Compare the local eye space, connections and liberties before and after a candidate point is occupied. Which of these can change?

u9-03.text: The same stones can lead to different outcomes depending on who moves next. Check whether the problem gives that condition.

u9-04.text: When groups join directly, ask which liberties and potential eye spaces they may share. That is different from a loose diagonal relationship.

u9-05.text: A sequence that works against one reply may fail against another. Look for a more forceful response to your first idea.

u9-06.text: A good early reading task has a defined local position and move order. Consider whether the suggested practice builds that skill gradually.

u10-01.text: Evaluate both orders of play in the boundary exchange. One side's gain alone does not capture the whole local swing.

u10-02.text: With safety and urgency equal, compare the actual score swing of each move rather than just the number of stones involved.

u10-03.text: One choice preserves the life of a corner group; the other earns ordinary endgame points. Reconsider what happens if the urgent move is delayed.

u10-04.text: Before calling a territorial count final, check whether any groups or boundaries still have unresolved status.

u10-05.text: Ask whether the opponent genuinely needs to answer the threat. The value of keeping initiative depends on that response.

u10-06.text: Find a concrete difference between the estimate and the final score. Could unsettled stones, borders or the scoring method explain it?

u11-01.text: Look away from the current fight long enough to check the safety of your group elsewhere. What happens if it receives no move now?

u11-02.text: Compare how much an unsettled area can change with a single move. An already secure area may offer little extra value.

u11-03.text: Consider both effects of the candidate: does it make your group safer, and does it also limit the opponent's useful space?

u11-04.text: A local capture has a cost elsewhere in the position. Compare your gain with the thickness the opponent develops outside.

u11-05.text: Scan for groups at risk, large unsettled areas and moves that cannot be postponed. These are different reasons for urgency.

u11-06.text: A familiar coordinate can be useful in one opening and poor in another. Check the relationships between groups before choosing direction.

u12-01.text: Compare the stones given up with the strength and opportunities gained outside. Avoid deciding solely from the number of captured stones.

u12-02.text: A forcing move has value only if the answer matters. Reconsider whether the opponent needs to respond and what you can play next.

u12-03.text: An invasion needs a credible plan after the opponent answers. Inspect connections, escape routes and potential eye space.

u12-04.text: Strong friendly stones nearby can support an attack. What useful gain could your pressure make even if the target escapes?

u12-05.text: Before adding another rescue stone, estimate what happens if it is also captured. Compare that cost with leaving the group.

u12-06.text: Look for the move when the fight stopped being safe for your group. A review question should identify an observable turning point.

u13-01.text: A ko threat is meant to demand a response. Ask how costly it would be for the opponent to ignore the move you are considering.

u13-02.text: Compare the position if either player wins the ko. The cost of threats makes sense only against the value at stake.

u13-03.text: The threat and the ko are two parts of the same exchange. Revisit what your opponent gains when responding to the larger threat.

u13-04.text: A potential ko threat must matter to the opponent. Look for vulnerable groups, territory or connections rather than a harmless move.

u13-05.text: The move away from the ko is not the end of the fight. Consider what reply it seeks and what opportunity may follow.

u13-06.text: Include the moves played away from the ko when judging the exchange. The local capture alone does not give its total value.

u14-01.text: Recall why both players might accept a known corner exchange in a particular position. Does that make the sequence mandatory everywhere?

u14-02.text: Look beyond the corner at the supporting and opposing stones. The outside direction can change whether a variation makes sense.

u14-03.text: When the surrounding stones differ, the remembered sequence may serve a different purpose. Recheck each move's intention.

u14-04.text: The corner sequence may be complete while another group remains weak. Examine what follow-up problems the exchange leaves behind.

u14-05.text: Both immediate territory and outside potential can be useful. Compare which outcome helps the actual neighbouring groups.

u14-06.text: Try describing what each exchange accomplishes rather than reciting the coordinates. That gives you a way to assess new positions.

u15-01.text: Find a move where group safety, territory or direction changed noticeably. Spending equal time on every move may hide that moment.

u15-02.text: If you record your own reasoning before reading suggestions, you can later compare the two accounts. Think about what that reveals.

u15-03.text: A tool's estimate is a candidate to investigate. Check which board problem the suggestion addresses instead of accepting its coordinate on authority.

u15-04.text: Choose one decision you could practise and observe in the next game. Trying to repair every mistake at once may not be actionable.

u15-05.text: A win or loss does not capture every behaviour in the game. Reconsider which specific decision improved and what still needs testing.

u15-06.text: Leave the review with a question about a turning point and something to check next time, rather than only a result or screenshot.
